title: The Great Depression
tagline: The causes of the worldwide slump after 1929 and its political consequences for democracy and extremism.

overview.intro: The Great Depression was the most severe economic collapse of the modern period, beginning in the United States in 1929 and spreading through the world through the banking system and the collapse of trade. This unit examines the structural weaknesses that made the slump so deep, the events through which it propagated from Wall Street to the rest of the world, and its political consequences: unemployment on a scale unknown in normal times, the decline of democratic governments and the rise of extremist movements that used the crisis to destroy the order that had produced it.

facts.label: Starting point
facts.value: The Wall Street crash of October 1929, with the market collapsing over late October.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: World trade fell by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934; unemployment reached about a third of the workforce in Germany and the United States.

facts.label: Banking crisis
facts.value: Thousands of banks failed in the United States in 1930–33, destroying savings and contracting credit.

facts.label: Political effect
facts.value: Collapse of coalition governments in Germany, adoption of protectionism, and the advance of extremist parties.

learningOutcomes: Explain the causes of the Great Depression.
Trace how the collapse in the United States spread to the rest of the world.
Describe the impact of unemployment and the fall in trade.
Assess the political consequences of the Depression for democracy.

blocks.text: The prosperity of the 1920s in the United States rested on fragile foundations. Production had expanded faster than the ability of consumers to buy, and wages did not keep pace with output, so goods accumulated unsold. A large part of consumer purchases and nearly all share purchases were made on credit, which meant that the boom depended on continued confidence. Speculation on the stock market drew in ordinary savers, with shares bought on margin, that is, on a small deposit and borrowed money, so a fall in prices could wipe out a holder immediately and force a sale.

Underneath lay structural weaknesses in the wider world economy. The First World War had left European economies dependent on American loans, and German reparations payments depended on American credit in a circular arrangement that stopped the moment the money stopped. Agricultural prices had been falling since the early 1920s, hitting the primary producers who supplied the raw materials and food that financed their imports. The gold standard transmitted deflation from country to country by requiring governments to raise interest rates and cut spending to protect their currency, which deepened the slump exactly where it was needed least.

blocks.text: The Wall Street crash of October 1929 destroyed confidence and with it the flow of American loans abroad. European banks that had borrowed short-term in New York to lend in Europe were recalled, and as they called in their own loans, German and Austrian firms and governments that depended on them were starved of credit. A wave of bank failures followed: in the United States thousands of banks collapsed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of ordinary depositors and shrinking the money supply further, and the failure of the Creditanstalt bank in Austria in May 1931 spread the crisis across the continent.

The policy response made matters worse. Governments raised tariffs to protect domestic producers, and the United States passed the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930, which was answered by retaliatory duties elsewhere. World trade, already falling, collapsed by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934. Countries left the gold standard in turn, Britain in 1931 and the United States in 1933, which devalued their currencies and gave some relief, but the competitive devaluations and tariff walls left the world economy divided into hostile blocs. Industrial production fell by about a third internationally, and in some countries the fall was steeper.

blocks.text: The human cost was unprecedented in peacetime. In the United States unemployment reached about a third of the labour force, with whole regions of industry idle and families dependent on relief lines that were both inadequate and humiliating. In Germany unemployment exceeded six million by 1932, close to a third of the workforce, and banks, savings and small businesses failed around it. In Britain, where the slump was less severe, unemployment remained above two million for years and the export industries of the north and midlands were depressed throughout the decade.

Governments responded with public works, relief payments and attempts to balance budgets, and the results varied. The New Deal in the United States from 1933 combined relief, recovery and reform through banking regulation, public employment and social security, and while it eased hardship and restored confidence it did not end unemployment before the war. Countries that left the gold standard early recovered earlier, and those that balanced budgets by cutting spending deepened the slump. The depression demonstrated that a modern economy could fail on a scale that neither the classical economic orthodoxy nor the political institutions of the day had anticipated.

items: Unemployment reached about a third of the labour force in the United States and Germany.
Bank failures destroyed savings and further contracted the money supply.
World trade fell by about two thirds between 1929 and 1934.
Public works and relief programmes were the standard response, with uneven results.
Recovery was faster where the gold standard was abandoned early.
The social effects included migration, falling birth rates and political radicalisation.

blocks.text: The Depression struck at democratic government. Coalition governments in Germany proved unable to respond to mass unemployment, and from 1930 rule by presidential emergency decree replaced parliamentary majorities, which hollowed out the republic before Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. The communist parties, taking their line from Moscow, treated social democrats as the main enemy and split the left at the moment unity was most needed. In Japan the crisis strengthened the hand of those who argued that expansion on the continent would solve the country’s economic problems.

The response of established governments was protection, and the consequence was a world economy divided into rival currency and trading blocs: a sterling area centred on Britain, a bloc around the United States, and a continental European system under German influence. The failure of international cooperation, visible in the breakdown of the World Economic Conference of 1933, meant that recovery was slow and that the economic nationalism of the 1930s fed directly into the political confrontation of the later decade. Historians differ on how direct the connection is: some argue that the Depression made the rise of extremism almost inevitable, others that in countries where democratic institutions had deeper roots, as in Britain and the United States, the same economic crisis produced reform rather than dictatorship. What is not disputed is that the crisis destroyed the international economic order of the 1920s and that the order that replaced it was shaped by the attempt to escape the slump.

keyPoints: Overproduction, weak wages and credit-fuelled speculation made the 1920s boom fragile.
The war-debt and reparations structure tied Europe to American credit.
The Wall Street crash of October 1929 stopped the flow of American loans abroad.
Bank failures in the United States and the collapse of the Creditanstalt spread the crisis.
Retaliatory tariffs after Smoot-Hawley cut world trade by about two thirds by 1934.
Unemployment reached about a third of the workforce in the United States and Germany.
The gold standard transmitted deflation and forced deflationary policies.
German democracy collapsed under emergency rule from 1930 before Hitler became chancellor.
The New Deal combined relief, recovery and reform from 1933.
Economic blocs and failed international cooperation shaped the politics of the 1930s.

questions.answer: The Wall Street crash of October 1929
questions.explanation: The crash destroyed confidence and stopped American lending, which set off the international collapse.

questions.explanation: Retaliatory tariffs following Smoot-Hawley cut world trade by about two thirds by 1934.

questions.prompt: The gold standard deepened the Depression because it:
options: Forced governments to raise interest rates and cut spending
questions.answer: Forced governments to raise interest rates and cut spending
questions.explanation: Defending currency convertibility required deflationary measures, which reduced demand exactly when it was needed.

questions.prompt: World trade fell by about two __________ between 1929 and 1934.
questions.explanation: The collapse reflected tariff barriers, the contraction of credit and the break-up of trading blocs.

questions.prompt: The American relief and recovery programme introduced from 1933 by President Roosevelt is called the New __________ .
questions.explanation: It combined relief for the unemployed, recovery measures and permanent banking and social reform.

questions.prompt: State four causes of the Great Depression.
questions.answer: Four causes are: overproduction combined with wages that lagged behind output, so goods could not be sold; the heavy use of credit and margin buying, which made prices vulnerable to a fall in confidence; the dependence of European economies on American short-term loans and the linked structure of war debts and reparations; and falling agricultural prices since the early 1920s, which reduced the income of primary producers. The gold standard is also accepted as a cause that transmitted deflation.
questions.explanation: Each cause must explain the mechanism by which it weakened the economy before the crash.

questions.prompt: Explain how the American banking crisis of 1930–33 affected the rest of the world.
questions.answer: When American banks failed in large numbers between 1930 and 1933 they lost the capacity to lend abroad, and they recalled the short-term loans that European banks and governments depended on. European institutions that had borrowed in New York to lend at home were forced to call in their own advances, which brought failures in Europe as well, the clearest example being the collapse of the Creditanstalt in Austria in May 1931. The destruction of savings and the contraction of the money supply reduced demand for imports, so the effect moved from the financial sector to trade. The result was that a domestic American crisis became a worldwide contraction of credit, output and trade.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the chain from bank failure to recalled loans to European failure to reduced trade, not just the fact of failure.

questions.prompt: Explain the causes of the Great Depression and describe its impact on unemployment.
questions.answer: The causes fall into two groups, the structural weaknesses of the 1920s and the event that exposed them. Production had grown faster than purchasing power, so inventories accumulated, and much consumption and nearly all share speculation was conducted on credit, which made prices depend on continued confidence. The European settlement of the war tied the continent to American loans, since German reparations and European rebuilding both depended on continuing credit from New York, and agricultural prices had been falling since the early 1920s, reducing the income of primary producers. The gold standard then converted a contraction into a worldwide deflation by requiring austerity to defend currencies. Against this background the Wall Street crash of October 1929 stopped American lending, European banks lost their funding, thousands of banks failed on both sides of the Atlantic, and tariff retaliation cut world trade by about two thirds by 1934. The impact on unemployment was severe and long-lasting: in the United States about a third of the labour force was out of work at the depth of the crisis, in Germany over six million were unemployed by 1932, and in Britain unemployment stayed above two million through much of the decade. Savings were wiped out by bank failures, industrial production fell by about a third internationally, and governments were forced into relief and public works programmes on a scale previously unknown.
questions.explanation: Full marks need causes grouped by mechanism and unemployment figures given with their source country and year.

questions.prompt: Did the Great Depression make the collapse of democracy inevitable? Answer with evidence from more than one country.
questions.answer: The case for inevitability rests first on scale: unemployment of about a third of the workforce removed the means by which citizens supported the republican order, and where governments tried to balance budgets by cutting spending, as Germany did, the contraction fed on itself. The German record is the strongest evidence, since parliamentary coalitions proved unable to command a majority after 1930, emergency presidential rule replaced normal government, and the Nazis became the largest party in 1932 before Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. Economic nationalism, tariff blocs and failed international cooperation narrowed the room for any democratic government to act. The case against inevitability is equally concrete. The same crisis in Britain produced the formation of a national government, the abandonment of the gold standard and eventually the welfare state, without dictatorship. In the United States the New Deal responded to the crisis through reform, banking regulation and public employment while constitutional government continued. In these countries democratic institutions had deeper roots, a broader consensus and greater resources, which suggests that the Depression was a stress test rather than a verdict: it destroyed the Weimar Republic because that republic was young, unsupported and institutionally incomplete, while older democracies absorbed the same shock. The judgement is therefore that the Depression made democratic failure highly likely where institutions were weak, but that it determined outcomes only in conjunction with the political structure it acted upon.
questions.explanation: Full marks require evidence from at least two countries and a judgement that distinguishes economic severity from institutional resilience.
